headline: 5 Unusual Things The Supreme Court Will Now Require A 'Detailed Relocation Plan' For
body:
1. The migration of the national collection of half-empty ballpoint pens from the current parliamentary stationery cupboard to a climate-controlled vault in South Delhi.
2. A comprehensive 800-page dossier detailing the exact logistical route for shifting the 'Resident Office Cat' from the North Block parking lot to its new designated sunbeam in the Ministry of Finance.
3. The systematic transfer of all unread internal memos and 'pending' files currently being used by staff as makeshift coasters, requiring a forensic audit of current liquid rings.
4. A structural stability report on the government's communal microwave oven, specifically assessing its ability to withstand the stress of a cross-town relocation without losing its ability to make samosas soggy.
5. An elaborate, phased decommissioning ceremony for the office water cooler, complete with a formal exit interview for the last person to have taken a drink from the original reservoir.
caption: Planning to move? Better start drafting your 500-page affidavit before you even touch that stapler. The judiciary has officially entered its 'logistics manager' era. #SupremeCourt #Bureaucracy #OfficeLife #Relocation (satire)
igHook: Tag a friend who would literally file a Supreme Court petition to avoid helping you move your couch.
imagePrompt: A large, dusty stack of cardboard moving boxes piled haphazardly in the middle of a grand, high-ceilinged colonial-era government office hallway.

sourceHeadline.title: Supreme Court seeks detailed plan from government on proposed relocation of Central Secretariat Library

judgeVerdict.reasoning: Candidate 11 strikes the best balance of specific, vivid bureaucratic absurdity (soggy samosas, liquid rings from coffee mugs) and maintains a warm, observant tone about office culture rather than descending into pure cynicism. It adheres strictly to the structural requirements while offering the most creative and visually distinct list of items.

safetyVerdict.reasoning: The article uses absurd, satirical premises to mock bureaucratic processes. It does not name any real individuals, target protected groups, or make defamatory claims against identifiable entities.
